text:
OPERATING SYSTEMS (UE24CS242B)
Unit 1 – Introduction & Computer System Organization

Operating Systems (OS) form the backbone of modern computing systems. Every application program, from a simple calculator to complex AI software, relies on the operating system to interact with the hardware. Without an operating system, application developers would need to write hardware-specific code, making software development extremely complex and impractical.

If an operating system were not developed, application developers would need to directly interact with hardware components such as the CPU, memory, disk, and I/O devices. This would require detailed knowledge of hardware architecture, device protocols, and low-level instructions.
The operating system abstracts hardware complexity and provides a standardized interface, allowing developers to focus on solving problems rather than managing hardware.

section_title: General Definition of an Operating System
text:
An Operating System is a program that acts as an intermediary between the user and the computer hardware.
It provides a user-friendly environment in which users can easily develop and execute programs.
Without an operating system:
• Hardware knowledge would be mandatory for programming
• Software portability would be extremely limited
• Resource conflicts would be difficult to manage

Early computers did not have operating systems. Programs were loaded manually, and only one program could run at a time. Over time, as hardware became more powerful and users demanded multitasking, operating systems evolved to manage resources efficiently and provide better usability.

The primary goals of an operating system are:
• Execute user programs and make solving user problems easier
• Make the computer system convenient to use
• Use hardware efficiently
• Manage system resources, including:
o Memory
o Processor(s)
o Input/Output devices
An effective OS balances user convenience with efficient hardware utilization.
Why Study Operating Systems?
Although only a small percentage of computer professionals design or modify operating systems, almost all software runs on top of an OS.
Understanding operating systems is crucial for:
• Writing efficient programs
• Developing secure applications
• Debugging performance issues
• Understanding resource behavior such as memory usage and CPU scheduling
Knowledge of OS fundamentals leads to proper, efficient, effective, and secure programming.

section_title: Four Components of a Computer System (Abstract View)
text:
A computer system can be divided into four major components:
1. Hardware - Provides basic computing resources such as:
o CPU
o Main memory
o I/O devices
2. Operating System - Controls and coordinates the use of hardware among various applications and users.
3. Application Programs - Define how system resources are used to solve user problems Examples:
o Word processors
o Compilers
o Web browsers
o Database systems
o Video games
4. Users - Can be people, machines, or other computers.
The operating system sits between hardware and application programs, ensuring safe and efficient usage of system resources.

section_title: What Operating Systems Do (User vs System View)
text:
From the user’s perspective:
• Desire convenience
• Want ease of use
• Expect good performance
• Do not care much about resource utilization
From the system’s perspective:
• Especially in shared systems (mainframes, minicomputers)
• Must ensure fair resource allocation
• Must maximize utilization of:
o CPU time
o Memory
o I/O devices
• No single user should monopolize resources

Dedicated systems (workstations): Have dedicated resources but still rely on shared
• servers (file, print, compute servers)
• Handheld devices: Resource-constrained, optimized for:
o Battery life
o Usability
Embedded systems:
Often have little or no user interface
• Examples:
o Automobiles
o Medical devices
o Home appliances
Operating systems are designed to balance usability and resource efficiency based on the system type.

From a system viewpoint, the operating system serves two major roles:
1. Resource Allocator
o Manages all system resources
o Resolves conflicting resource requests
o Ensures fairness and efficiency
2. Control Program
o Controls execution of programs
o Prevents errors
o Prevents improper use of the computer

The fundamental goal of a computer system is to execute user programs and solve user problems.
The operating system combines:
• Resource allocation
• Control mechanisms into a single piece of software.
The kernel is:
• The core part of the OS
• The only program running at all times
Everything else is either:
• A system program (ships with OS)
• An application program

A computer system consists of:
• One or more CPUs
• Device controllers
• Shared main memory
• Common system bus
The CPU and device controllers can execute concurrently, competing for memory cycles. A memory controller synchronizes access to shared memory.
A Modern Computer System
Modern systems support parallelism, concurrency, and high-speed I/O operations.

Key points:
• CPU and I/O devices execute concurrently
• Each device controller manages a specific device
• Device controller contains:
o Local buffer
o Registers for control actions
• Data transfer occurs:
o Device → Controller buffer → Main memory
After completing an operation, the device controller signals the CPU by generating an interrupt.

When the system starts:
• The first program executed is the Bootstrap program
• Stored in ROM or EEPROM
• Also called firmware
Functions of bootstrap:
• Initializes CPU registers
• Initializes memory
• Initializes device controllers
• Loads the operating system kernel into memory
After booting:
• The first user-level process created is init init waits for events and starts system services

An operating system is interrupt-driven.
• Interrupt transfers control to an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)
• Uses an interrupt vector containing addresses of service routines
• CPU state (program counter, registers) is saved
A trap or exception is a software-generated interrupt caused by:
• Errors
• User requests (system calls)

Steps in interrupt handling:
1. Save current CPU state
2. Identify interrupt type
3. Execute appropriate interrupt service routine
4. Restore CPU state
5. Resume execution
Interrupt identification methods:
• Polling
• Vectored interrupt systems
Shows how a single process performing output is interrupted and resumed.

Main memory:
• Only large storage directly accessible by CPU
• Random Access Memory (RAM)
• Typically volatile
Implemented using DRAM.
Other memory types:
• ROM
• EEPROM (used in smartphones to store factory-installed programs)

Typical instruction execution follows the Fetch–Decode–Execute cycle:
1. Fetch instruction from memory
2. Decode instruction
3. Execute instruction
This repeats until program termination.
This model is known as the Von Neumann architecture.

Secondary storage:
• Extension of main memory
• Non-volatile
• Large capacity
Types:
• Hard disks
o Platters, tracks, sectors
o Managed by disk controller
• Solid State Drives (SSD)
o Faster
o Non-volatile
• Flash memory
o Used in cameras, PDAs

Storage systems are organized based on:
• Speed
• Cost
• Volatility

Caching is a fundamental principle used at many levels:
• Hardware
• Operating system
• Software
Key ideas:
• Frequently used data copied to faster storage
• Cache checked first
• If data not present → fetched from slower storage
Challenges:
• Cache size
• Replacement policy
• Cache management

• Storage is treated as an I/O device
• Large portion of OS code manages I/O
• Focus on reliability and performance
Components:
• CPUs
• Multiple device controllers
• Common system bus
Each device controller has:
• Device driver
• Uniform interface to kernel

• Device controller maintains local buffer
• Transfers data between device and memory
• CPU resumes execution after I/O completion interrupt
Two models:
1. CPU waits for I/O completion
2. CPU continues execution while I/O proceeds

Used for high-speed I/O devices.
• Data transferred directly between device and main memory
• CPU involvement minimized
• Only one interrupt per block transfer
Improves performance significantly.

OPERATING SYSTEMS (UE24CS242B)
Unit 1 – CPU Scheduling

In a computer system with a single CPU core, only one process can execute at a time. All other processes must wait until the CPU becomes free and they are scheduled again.
The main objective of multiprogramming is to:
• Keep the CPU busy at all times
• Maximize CPU utilization
To achieve this:
• Several processes are kept in main memory
• When one process has to wait (usually for I/O), the OS:
o Takes the CPU away from that process
o Assigns the CPU to another ready process
This cycle continues, ensuring that the CPU rarely remains idle.

On a multicore system, the same concept is extended:
• Each processing core should be kept busy
• Scheduling decisions are made independently for each core
• Improves overall system throughput and performance

In a simple system without multiprogramming:
• A process executes until it must wait (typically for I/O)
• During this waiting period, the CPU remains idle
• CPU time is wasted and no useful work is done
Multiprogramming allows the OS to:
• Switch the CPU to another ready process
• Use waiting time productively
This makes CPU scheduling a fundamental OS function.

section_title: Alternating Sequence of CPU and I/O Bursts
text:
Process execution consists of an alternating sequence of CPU bursts and I/O bursts.
• CPU burst → process is executing instructions
• I/O burst → process is waiting for I/O completion
Maximum CPU utilization is achieved when:
• CPU bursts of one process overlap with I/O bursts of another

• Execution pattern:
o CPU burst → I/O burst → CPU burst → I/O burst → …
• CPU scheduling algorithms focus mainly on:
o The distribution of CPU burst times
Understanding this cycle is essential for designing efficient schedulers.

The duration of CPU bursts:
• Varies widely among processes
• Follows a characteristic frequency distribution

• I/O-bound processes
o Many short CPU bursts
• CPU-bound processes
o Few long CPU bursts
This distribution is important when:
• Designing
• Evaluating
• Comparing CPU scheduling algorithms

The CPU scheduler (short-term scheduler):
• Selects a process from the ready queue
• Allocates the CPU to that process

The ready queue may be organized in various ways:
• FIFO queue
• Priority queue
• Tree
• Unordered linked list
Each entry in the queue is a Process Control Block (PCB).

CPU scheduling decisions can occur when a process:
1. Switches from running → waiting
2. Switches from running → ready
3. Switches from waiting → ready
4. Terminates

• Cases 1 and 4 → Non-preemptive
• Cases 2 and 3 → Preemptive

When preemption occurs:
• Shared data access must be handled carefully
• Preemption while executing in kernel mode must be considered
• Interrupts may occur during critical OS operations

• Windows 3.x → Non-preemptive
• Windows 95 onwards → Preemptive
• Macintosh OS → Uses preemptive scheduling

• Can cause race conditions
• Occurs when:
o One process is preempted while updating shared data
o Another process accesses inconsistent data

• Preemptive kernels use:
o Mutex locks
o Other synchronization mechanisms
Most modern operating systems are:
• Fully preemptive, even in kernel mode

The dispatcher is a module that:
• Gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler

• Performs context switch
• Switches CPU to user mode
• Jumps to the correct location in the user program

• Time taken to:
o Stop one process
o Start another process
• Important performance metric

Scheduling algorithms are evaluated based on the following criteria:
1. CPU Utilization
o Percentage of time CPU is busy
2. Throughput
o Number of processes completed per unit time
3. Turnaround Time
o Time from submission to completion of a process
4. Waiting Time
o Total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue
5. Response Time
o Time from request submission to first response
o Important in time-sharing systems

An ideal scheduling algorithm should aim to:
• Maximize
o CPU utilization
o Throughput
• Minimize
o Turnaround time
o Waiting time
o Response time
Different scheduling algorithms optimize different criteria based on system goals.

OPERATING SYSTEMS (UE24CS242B)
Unit 1 – Process Concept (Process Management)

An operating system executes a variety of programs:
• Batch systems → execute jobs
• Time-shared systems → execute user programs or tasks
In operating-system literature, the terms job and process are often used interchangeably.

• A program is a passive entity
o Stored on disk as an executable file
• A process is an active entity
o A program in execution
A program becomes a process when:
• Its executable file is loaded into memory
• Execution begins (via GUI click, command line, script, etc.)

section_title: One program can have multiple processes
text: • Example: Multiple users running the same editor simultaneously

A process consists of several parts in memory:
1. Text Section
o Program code
o Instructions to be executed
2. Current Activity
o Program Counter
o Processor Registers
3. Stack
o Temporary data
o Function parameters
o Return addresses
o Local variables
4. Data Section
o Global and static variables
5. Heap
o Dynamically allocated memory during runtime

section_title: Memory Layout of a C Program
text:
This layout explains how different segments of a program are organized in memory during execution.
Memory Layout of a Process
As a process executes, it changes state.

1. New
o Process is being created
2. Running
o Instructions are currently being executed
3. Waiting
o Process is waiting for an event (e.g., I/O completion)
4. Ready
o Process is waiting to be assigned to a CPU
5. Terminated
o Process has finished execution

Each process is represented in the operating system by a Process Control Block (PCB)
(also called Task Control Block).

• The PCB contains all information needed to manage a process:
o New, ready, running, waiting, terminated
• Program counter
o Address of next instruction to execute
• CPU registers
o Contents of all process-specific registers
• CPU scheduling information
o Priority
o Scheduling queue pointers
• Memory-management information
o Memory allocated to the process
• Accounting information
o CPU time used
o Elapsed time
o Time limits
• I/O status information
o I/O devices allocated
o List of open files

section_title: CPU Switch from Process to Process
text: When the CPU changes from executing one process to another, the system performs a context switch.

The objective of process scheduling is to:
• Maximize CPU utilization
• Support time sharing
• Ensure fairness among processes
A process scheduler selects a process for execution on the CPU.

The operating system maintains several scheduling queues:
1. Job Queue
o All processes in the system
2. Ready Queue
o Processes in main memory
o Ready to execute
3. Device Queues
o Processes waiting for I/O devices
Processes migrate among these queues during execution.

section_title: Ready Queue and I/O Device Queues
text: Representation of Process Scheduling

• Selects the next process to execute on the CPU
• Invoked very frequently (milliseconds)
• Must be extremely fast
• Often the only scheduler in a system

• Selects processes to be admitted into the ready queue
• Invoked infrequently (seconds or minutes)
• Controls the degree of multiprogramming
• May be slow

Processes are broadly classified as:
1. I/O-Bound Process
o Spends more time doing I/O
o Many short CPU bursts
2. CPU-Bound Process
o Spends more time doing computation
o Few long CPU bursts
The long-term scheduler tries to maintain a good mix of both.

A medium-term scheduler may be introduced to:
• Reduce the degree of multiprogramming

• Process is removed from memory
• Stored on disk
• Later brought back to continue execution

A context switch occurs when:
• CPU switches from one process to another
Steps involved:
1. Save the state of the current process in its PCB
2. Load the saved state of the next process

• Context switch time is overhead
• No useful work is done during switching
• Time depends on:
o Hardware support
o PCB complexity
• Some CPUs support multiple register sets to reduce switch time
• The operating system must provide mechanisms for:

• A parent process can create child processes
• Child processes may create further processes
• Forms a process tree
Each process is identified by a Process ID (PID).

• Parent and child share all resources
• Child shares a subset of parent’s resources
• Parent and child share no resources

• Parent and child execute concurrently
• Parent waits until child terminates
Process Creation using fork() fork() creates a new process
• Child process is a duplicate of the parent
• Address space is copied
To run a different program: exec() is used
• Replaces the process memory with a new program
UNIX Example fork() → creates child process exec() → loads new program into child

A process terminates when:
• It executes its last statement
• Calls the exit() system call

• Status value returned from child to parent
• Parent retrieves status using wait()
• OS deallocates all process resources

Parent may terminate a child using abort() if:
• Child exceeds allocated resources
• Task assigned to child is no longer needed
• Parent itself is terminating

Some operating systems do not allow a child to exist without a parent.
• If parent terminates → all children terminate
• This is called cascading termination
• Initiated by the operating system

• Zombie process
o Child terminates
o Parent has not called wait()
• Orphan process
o Parent terminates before child
o Child is adopted by init/system process

• What happens if parent terminates before child?
• What happens if child terminates before parent (parent sleeping)?
• How to determine the state of a process?
These are handled using process tables and system calls like wait().
